transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because I can’t stop noticing how droopy and uneven my mouth and jaw look. In photos, reflections—everywhere. People tell me I look fine, but it seems so obvious to me. It’s gotten to where I avoid presentations and meeting with clients.
Roughly how many hours a day would you say you spend thinking about your mouth and jaw?

Honestly, several hours a day—probably most of the day in one way or another. I keep noticing the droop and unevenness around my mouth and jaw in photos or reflections, and then I can’t stop thinking about it.
Do you find yourself doing things repeatedly because of these thoughts, such as checking mirrors, trying to hide or fix your jaw, or comparing yourself to others?

Yes. Before work or a family event, I can spend hours in the bathroom mirror, taking pictures of my face from different angles and redoing my makeup or adjusting my scarf. I ask my husband over and over if my face looks lopsided. Then I end up scrolling through photos of other women and comparing myself to them.
Deep down, do you think it's possible that your view of your face might be distorted or exaggerated, or are you completely convinced that it looks exactly as bad as you see it?
I’m not sure what you mean by distorted. I know other people say they don’t see it, but when I look at my face, the unevenness looks very real to me.
Is there any room in your mind to doubt what you see, or are you completely certain that your mouth and jaw are physically deformed?

I mean, people tell me I look fine, so I suppose there could be something I’m not seeing the same way. But when I look in a photo or reflection, the droop and unevenness around my mouth and jaw are so obvious to me. I can’t stop noticing it, and it’s gotten to where I avoid presentations and meeting with clients because of it.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with prominent, distressing preoccupation with a perceived physical defect (droopy and uneven mouth and jaw) that is not observable or barely noticeable to others. This preoccupation occupies several hours daily and leads to repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, camouflage with makeup/scarves, taking photos, reassurance seeking, comparing appearance with others) and causes clinically significant functional impairment (avoiding client meetings and presentations). In ICD-10, body dysmorphic disorder (dysmorphophobia) is classified under F45.2.

confirmed_symptoms: Preoccupation with perceived droopy and uneven mouth and jaw
Obsessive thoughts taking up several hours/most of the day
Repeated mirror checking and taking photos from different angles
Compulsive social comparison with photos of others

additional_requirements: Non-delusional belief confirmed with capacity for doubt regarding perceived defect
Avoidance of work-related activities (presentations, meeting with clients)
